passage:
Friday night. Karthik asked today, over dosa at the canteen: 'So what are we? I need to know where this is going.' My chest tightened like a door had shut. We've been seeing each other for four months. I like him a lot. I also don't know if I want something serious in my last year, with placements and maybe a move. My first instinct was to say 'yeah, obviously, serious,' just to make his face relax. Or to change the subject, like I did last week. I did neither. I said, 'I really like you. I'm sure about that. I'm not sure yet about long-term, because I don't know where I'll be after May. I don't want to promise something I can't keep.' He went quiet. Then he said, 'Okay. Thanks for not faking it.' We agreed to talk again after placements. I feel shaky, but honest. Better than stringing him along.
- Ujjwal

qa.q: When did Karthik and Ujjwal agree to talk again?
qa.a: After placements.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal feel when Karthik asked where this was going?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt cornered, the chest tightening like a door had shut.

qa.q: What was honest about Ujjwal's answer?
qa.a: Ujjwal said clearly what was certain (liking Karthik) and what wasn't (long-term plans), without faking a yes or dodging.

qa.q: How does Karthik take the honest answer?
qa.a: He goes quiet, then thanks Ujjwal for not faking it.

grounding: A diary of a young person asked to define a relationship, feeling cornered but answering honestly about what they do and don't know.

passage: In Bishnupur, Santosh had just signed the lease on his father's old sweet shop, while Bidisha's acceptance letter from a design school in Bengaluru sat on her kitchen table. Two years of evenings by the temple pond, and now their plans pointed in opposite directions. Santosh felt it for weeks before he said anything. He replied late and found excuses not to meet, half hoping she would end it so he wouldn't have to. Then one evening she asked, hurt, 'Are you pulling away?' His guilt flared. He sat down on the pond steps. 'Yes. And that's unfair to you. I'm staying here, Bidisha. This shop is my life. You're going to Bengaluru, and you should. I don't think we want the same things any more.' She cried. So did he. They talked till the temple bells rang. It ended that night, gently, with a hug. It hurt. But he didn't have to pretend any more, and neither did she.

qa.q: What had Santosh signed?
qa.a: The lease on his father's old sweet shop.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling as he replied late and avoided meeting?
qa.a: He felt guilty and torn, half hoping Bidisha would end it so he wouldn't have to.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Quiet withdrawal left Bidisha hurt and confused; talking honestly and ending it kindly was fairer.

qa.q: How does Bidisha experience Santosh's withdrawal?
qa.a: She feels hurt and unsure, which is why she finally asks if he is pulling away.

grounding: Shows a young man whose goals diverge from his partner's, moving from guilty withdrawal to an honest talk and a kind ending.

passage: Liam noticed it first in small things. Ada had started saving for a flat in Galway and talking about her sister's baby with a soft look. Liam had just applied for a two-year volunteer post in rural Peru, and hadn't told her. They had been together since the first week of university. He loved her. He also felt, more and more, as if they were rowing in different directions. The old Liam would have gone quiet and waited for the distance to decide for them. Instead, on a Sunday walk along the Liffey, he said, 'Ada, I applied for the Peru post. I should have told you. I think we want different lives, at least right now.' She stopped walking. 'I think I knew,' she said. They sat on a bench for two hours, crying and laughing about first-year disasters. They decided to end it, with care, before resentment could set in. He felt guilty for weeks. But not dishonest.

qa.q: Where had Liam applied to volunteer?
qa.a: For a two-year post in rural Peru.

qa.q: What did Liam feel in the weeks after they ended it?
qa.a: He felt guilty, though not dishonest.

qa.q: What did Liam do differently from 'the old Liam'?
qa.a: He told Ada about the application and their diverging goals early, instead of withdrawing and letting distance decide.

qa.q: How does Ada react to Liam's news?
qa.a: She stops walking and admits she thinks she already knew.

grounding: Shows a young man whose goals diverge from his partner's, choosing an honest early talk and a kind ending over quiet withdrawal.

passage:
'Can we talk about money for a minute?' Irawati asked, pushing the café bill across the table.
Tushar froze. 'Oh no. Did I forget my wallet again?'
'No. It's not that. It's... I've been paying for most things since my internship started. Dinners, movies, your birthday trip. And I've started keeping a list in my head. That's not fair to you, because I never said anything.'
Tushar went red. 'I didn't know you minded. I thought you liked treating me.'
'I did. Then I started expecting you to... I don't know, owe me. And that's not what I want either.'
'My scholarship is really tight. I've been embarrassed about it.'
'So let's just say it out loud. What can you manage each week?'
They wrote it on a napkin. Tushar would take the Friday dinners; Irawati would cover movies. Cheaper places, more walks.
'I don't want to buy you,' she said.
'And I don't want to be bought,' he laughed. 'Deal.'

qa.q: What did Irawati push across the table?
qa.a: The café bill.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling about paying for most things?
qa.a: She felt quietly resentful and uneasy, keeping a mental list and expecting Tushar to owe her.

qa.q: What did Irawati and Tushar agree to do?
qa.a: Say their budgets out loud and split what each could manage: Friday dinners for him, movies for her, plus cheaper outings 😊

qa.q: Why hadn't Tushar raised the money issue?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his tight scholarship.

grounding: Shows a young woman who pays more in a relationship and notices resentment, talking openly about money and respecting each other's budget.

passage: In my second year of college, I thought love meant gifts. I'm Gautam, and when I started dating Zeenat, I spent half my tutoring money on her: earrings for her birthday, a smartwatch for 'our three months', flowers delivered to her hostel. Part of me believed it would make her stay. Then one evening she handed the smartwatch back, very gently. 'Gautam, I can't match any of this. Every gift feels like a debt I'm supposed to pay back. I just want to walk with you after class.' I felt embarrassed and then, honestly, a bit hurt, as if I'd been refused. But she was right. I'd been trying to buy something that can't be bought, and it made her feel obliged instead of loved. We talked properly that night about money: what I earned, what she had, what we were each comfortable spending. Now our dates are mostly chai and long walks by the lake. Strangely, we're closer than ever.

qa.q: What did Zeenat hand back to Gautam?
qa.a: The smartwatch.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when Zeenat returned the watch?
qa.a: Gautam felt embarrassed and then a bit hurt, as if being refused.

qa.q: What changed after they talked about money?
qa.a: They agreed on what each was comfortable spending, and dates became chai and long walks by the lake.

qa.q: How did the gifts make Zeenat feel?
qa.a: Obliged rather than loved, as if every gift were a debt to repay.

grounding: A first-person account of trying to buy love with gifts, learning from a partner's discomfort and talking openly about money and budgets.

passage: College counsellor's note, Thursday. Rekha (second year, commerce) came in upset after a fight with her boyfriend, Akash. She said he refused to post an anniversary photo, and she felt he was 'hiding' her. When I asked what posting meant to her, she scrolled through the couple accounts she follows: matching outfits, surprise videos, captions of eternal love. She admitted she'd been comparing their relationship with these every night and feeling it came up short. We looked at her own last month instead: long phone calls when her grandmother was ill, Akash waiting outside her exam hall, cooking together at his aunt's. She went quiet, then said, 'The good stuff wasn't online at all.' She decided to talk to Akash about why the photo had mattered to her, and to mute the couple accounts for a while. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rekha fight with Akash?
qa.a: He refused to post an anniversary photo.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after comparing her relationship with couple accounts?
qa.a: She felt insecure and let down, as if their relationship came up short.

qa.q: What did Rekha decide after the session?
qa.a: To talk to Akash about why the photo mattered and to mute the couple accounts for a while.

qa.q: How might Akash see the anniversary photo fight?
qa.a: He may feel accused of hiding Rekha when he values private moments like waiting outside her exam hall.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a young woman wanting her relationship validated online, noticing that posts were replacing rather than reflecting closeness.

passage:
Sunday night. Today Jaya and I went to the lake for our one-year anniversary. I spent the first hour setting up photos: the right light, the boat, the matching coffee cups. I made her redo a 'candid' laugh four times. Then I posted it and kept refreshing to see who liked it. At some point I looked up and Jaya was just sitting on the bench, watching the ducks, a bit quiet. I asked if she was okay. She said, 'I miss you. You've been here all day but not really.' That hit hard. I'd been performing us instead of being with her. I scrolled back through my posts and saw that every single one was from a moment I don't really remember. I put the phone in my bag. We fed the ducks, talked about her new job, shared some terrible samosas. No photos. It was the best part of the day.
- Ishita

qa.q: How many times did Ishita make Jaya redo the 'candid' laugh?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What did Ishita feel when Jaya said 'I miss you'?
qa.a: Ishita felt a hard jolt of guilt, realising the day had gone on performing instead of being together.

qa.q: What did Ishita do to change the rest of the day?
qa.a: Put the phone away and simply fed the ducks, talked and shared samosas with Jaya, with no photos 🙂

qa.q: How was the day for Jaya before the phone went away?
qa.a: Lonely, with Ishita there all day but not really present.

grounding: A diary of a young person who notices anniversary posts replacing closeness, and puts the phone away to be present.

passage: Dolma, you asked why I wanted six more months before the engagement. Sit, it's a whole thing. I'm Yamini, and when Arvind's parents came to meet mine, everything went fast. By dessert the aunties were talking dates and halls, and I just kept nodding, because everyone looked so happy. That night I lay awake and realised we'd never talked about the big things. Would I keep working after marriage? His mother had said 'of course she'll adjust' at dinner. Would we live with his parents? Kids, when? Did he even want them? So the next weekend Arvind and I sat in a quiet café with a list. Some answers matched. Some didn't: he assumed we'd move in with his parents; I'd assumed not. We didn't fight. We just saw we needed time. When I asked both families for six months, my mother was upset for a day. Arvind backed me. I'd rather be sure than be agreeable.

qa.q: What did Arvind's mother say at dinner?
qa.a: 'Of course she'll adjust.'

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she lay awake after the families met?
qa.a: Yamini felt uneasy and rushed, realising the big questions had never been discussed.

qa.q: What did Yamini and Arvind do before agreeing to dates?
qa.a: They talked through a list of big questions, found where they differed, and asked for six more months.

qa.q: How did Yamini's mother react to the delay?
qa.a: She was upset for a day.

grounding: A spoken account of a young woman who pauses a rushed engagement to check shared values on work, parents and children with her partner.

passage: January. At the church hall in Aizawl, after the Sunday service, both families were beaming: Lalremsiami and Joseph should marry next December. Everyone agreed, so they agreed too. Siami smiled until her cheeks ached. March. Planning the guest list, Joseph mentioned that his mother expected them to move in with her, and that Siami would 'of course' leave her nursing job when the first baby came. Siami set down her pen. She had assumed none of that. That night she told him, 'We've said yes to everyone except each other. We need to talk properly.' Joseph looked stunned, then nodded. May. They had spent three long evenings on it: work, where to live, children, helping his younger brothers. Joseph agreed she would keep nursing; they'd live near his mother, not with her. Some things were still open. They moved the wedding to the following spring, and this time the yes felt like theirs.

qa.q: Where were the families when they agreed on a December wedding?
qa.a: At the church hall in Aizawl, after the Sunday service.

qa.q: What was Siami feeling when Joseph mentioned her leaving nursing?
qa.a: She felt shocked and uneasy, realising she had assumed none of what his family expected.

qa.q: What made the final decision stronger?
qa.a: Talking properly about work, living arrangements and children before setting a date, instead of agreeing to please everyone.

qa.q: How did Joseph respond when Siami said they needed to talk?
qa.a: He looked stunned at first, then agreed and worked through the questions with her.

grounding: Shows a young couple who move from agreeing to please their families to discussing work, parents and children before marrying.

passage: The first time I really felt it was at Jyoti's cousin's wedding. She was laughing, head thrown back, with a guy from her college I'd never met, and something hot shot up through my chest. I'm Uma, and I'm not proud of the next hour: I sulked by the dessert table, and in the car I almost asked for her phone password. I actually opened my mouth. Then I heard how it would sound: an accusation, as if she'd done something wrong. She hadn't. She'd laughed. So I took a breath and said something harder. 'Jyoti, when you were laughing with him, I felt really jealous. That's my insecurity, not something you did. I just didn't want to hide it and get weird.' She was quiet, then squeezed my hand. 'Thank you for telling me like that. He's a friend from debate. Want to meet him properly?' I did, later. He was nice. The jealousy shrank once I'd said it out loud.

qa.q: Where did Uma first feel the jealousy?
qa.a: At Jyoti's cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What did Uma feel watching Jyoti laugh with the guy from college?
qa.a: Uma felt a hot pang of jealousy shoot up through the chest.

qa.q: How did Uma share the jealousy in a healthy way?
qa.a: By naming it as Uma's own insecurity, not accusing Jyoti, instead of asking for her password.

qa.q: How does Jyoti respond to Uma's honesty?
qa.a: She thanks Uma for sharing it that way and offers an introduction to her debate friend.

grounding: A first-person account of feeling jealous when a partner laughs with someone else, and naming the insecurity instead of accusing or demanding passwords.

passage: Counselling note, Monday. Chaitanya (final year, mechanical) came in because, in his words, 'I'm turning into someone I don't like.' Over the weekend he saw his girlfriend Urmila joking with her lab partner and felt, as he put it, 'a hot punch in the stomach'. He then demanded her phone password and told her to switch lab partners. She refused and left. He said he felt ashamed afterwards. We explored where the jealousy came from: his last relationship ended when his ex cheated, and he has been bracing for it ever since. I pointed out the difference between the feeling, which is his and understandable, and the demands, which try to control Urmila. We practised a way to share it: 'When I saw you two laughing, I felt insecure. That's about my past, not you. Can we talk?' He plans to apologise for the password demand and share this instead. Follow-up next week.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya demand from Urmila?
qa.a: Her phone password, and that she switch lab partners.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after Urmila left?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of his demands.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya plan to do next?
qa.a: Apologise for the password demand and share his insecurity as his own feeling, not an accusation.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when Chaitanya demanded her password?
qa.a: Probably hurt and controlled, as if accused of something she hadn't done.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a young man whose jealousy turned into demands, learning to share the insecurity as a feeling instead of controlling his partner.

passage:
'Who's Priya?' Sunaina held up his phone, the message preview glowing.
Shankar kept his voice calm. 'My project partner. She's asking about the circuit diagram.'
'You text her every night.'
'About the project. You can read it if you want, this once. But I'm not going to stop talking to her.'
'Why not? If you loved me, you'd understand.'
He sat down beside her. 'I do love you. That's why I'm telling you straight. There's nothing going on. But I can't hide my friends or drop them to prove it. That's not trust, that's me shrinking.'
Sunaina looked away. 'I just get scared.'
'I know. You can tell me when you're scared. I'll listen. I'll reassure you. But I won't sneak around or cut people off.'
'And if I can't handle it?'
'Then we talk about it. Maybe with someone who can help. But the answer isn't me having no friends.'
She was quiet a long time. 'Okay. Show me the diagram.'

qa.q: Who is Priya, according to Shankar?
qa.a: His project partner, asking about the circuit diagram.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling as Sunaina held up his phone?
qa.a: He felt watched and uneasy, but kept his voice calm and steady.

qa.q: How did Shankar hold the line kindly?
qa.a: He reassured Sunaina once, offered to listen when she's scared, but refused to hide or drop friends to prove trust.

qa.q: What is Sunaina feeling underneath her questions?
qa.a: She is scared of losing him, which comes out as jealousy about Priya.

grounding: Shows a young man whose partner is jealous of his friends, reassuring her once while refusing to give up his freedom or hide people.

passage: For about four months in second year, I hid my own friends. I'm Nandini, and my boyfriend Tanvir would go silent for a whole day if I went out with my theatre group, especially if any of the guys were there. So I started lying. 'Just studying.' 'Just the girls.' I deleted group photos before he could see them. I felt watched all the time, even when he wasn't around. It was my friend Kavya who noticed. 'You've stopped showing up in any of our photos. Are you okay?' Saying it out loud made me see how small I'd made my life. So I talked to Tanvir. I told him once, clearly: 'I love you, and nothing is going on with anyone. But I'm not hiding my friends any more. Trust can't mean I give up my freedom.' He sulked. Then, after a week, he apologised and started seeing a counsellor about his jealousy. I went back to theatre. No more deleting photos.

qa.q: What did Nandini delete before Tanvir could see them?
qa.a: Group photos.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel during those four months of hiding?
qa.a: Nandini felt anxious and watched all the time, even when Tanvir wasn't around, living a shrunken life.

qa.q: What made Nandini's talk with Tanvir wise?
qa.a: Nandini reassured him once but held the line that trust doesn't mean giving up friends or freedom.

qa.q: How did Tanvir eventually respond?
qa.a: He sulked, then apologised after a week and started seeing a counsellor about his jealousy.

grounding: A first-person account of hiding friends to keep a jealous partner calm, then reassuring once and refusing to surrender freedom.

passage: I'm going to say something embarrassing, because I think someone listening needs it. I'm Hafsa, and last year I was a controlling girlfriend. I made Chetan share his live location 'for safety' and checked it constantly. I told him which shirts made other girls look at him. When he went on a trip with his school friends, I called eleven times in one night. I told myself this was love, that I cared more than other people did. Then one day Chetan said, very quietly, 'I feel like I'm on a leash.' I was furious for about an hour. Then I sat with it. Under all of it was fear: that if I didn't hold on tight, he'd disappear, the way my father did when I was nine. That wasn't Chetan's fault. He's his own person, not something I own. I apologised, stopped the location sharing, and started seeing a counsellor. We're still together. It's lighter now, for both of us.

qa.q: What did Hafsa make Chetan share?
qa.a: His live location, 'for safety'.

qa.q: What was Hafsa afraid of underneath the controlling?
qa.a: Hafsa was afraid Chetan would disappear the way her father did, a deep fear dressed up as love.

qa.q: What steps did Hafsa take once she saw the fear?
qa.a: Apologised, stopped the location sharing and started seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: How did Chetan experience Hafsa's control?
qa.a: He felt like he was on a leash.

grounding: A spoken account of a young woman recognising her possessiveness as fear, not love, and seeing her partner as a separate person.

passage: February. When Aparna joined the college trekking club, Disha felt a cold twist in her stomach. She started asking who else was going, what Aparna would wear, whether she'd share her location every hour. She told herself it was because she cared. March. After the first trek, Aparna came home glowing, full of stories about the new friends she'd made. Disha barely listened. Later she found herself scrolling through the club members' profiles, one by one, at 2 a.m. She stopped, shocked at herself. This wasn't care. It was fear of being left, dressed up as care. April. Disha told Aparna the truth over breakfast: 'I've been trying to control you because I'm scared. You're your own person. I'm sorry.' She booked a session at the student counselling centre. The next weekend, when Aparna left for the second trek, Disha packed her a tiffin and didn't ask for a single location update.

qa.q: What club did Aparna join?
qa.a: The college trekking club.

qa.q: What did Disha feel scrolling through profiles at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: She felt shocked at herself, recognising her fear of being left.

qa.q: What did Disha do once she recognised the pattern?
qa.a: Told Aparna the truth, apologised, booked counselling, and let her go on the next trek without location updates.

qa.q: How did Aparna come home from the first trek?
qa.a: Glowing and full of stories about new friends, excited about her own life.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose possessiveness grows over weeks until she sees it as fear, apologises and treats her partner as a separate person.

passage: By her second year at university in Manchester, Chidi had stopped going to the Nigerian society dinners. Siddiq said the guys there 'looked at her wrong'. She'd stopped wearing her yellow dress because he said it was 'for attention'. He checked her location 'because he loved her', and got upset if she took more than ten minutes to reply. Each rule came wrapped in a kiss or a worried face, so she told herself it was love. One afternoon her old flatmate Grace bumped into her in the library. 'Chidi! We never see you any more. Are you okay?' Chidi opened her mouth to say fine and, to her own surprise, started crying. Over coffee she listed the rules out loud and heard them properly for the first time. Grace said gently, 'That's not love, that's control. And it's not your fault.' That week, with Grace beside her, Chidi went to the university counselling service. She wore the yellow dress.

qa.q: What did Siddiq say about Chidi's yellow dress?
qa.a: That it was 'for attention'.

qa.q: What did Chidi feel when Grace asked if she was okay?
qa.a: She was surprised by her own tears, feeling the weight of how small her life had become.

qa.q: What helped Chidi start to see the pattern?
qa.a: Listing the rules out loud to Grace, hearing Grace name it as control, and going to the counselling service.

qa.q: How does Grace see Siddiq's rules?
qa.a: As control, not love, and she makes sure Chidi knows it isn't her fault.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose partner's control is framed as love, recognising the pattern with a friend and seeking counselling; it is not her fault.

passage: In the hostel common room, Raghav noticed Tushar checking his phone again, the fourth time in ten minutes, and switching seats so his back was to the TV where students from the girls' block were watching cricket. 'Kriti doesn't like me sitting near other girls,' Tushar muttered. Over the semester he'd quit the band, skipped Raghav's birthday, and sent Kriti a photo every hour to prove where he was. 'She just loves me a lot,' he always said. That night Raghav said quietly, 'Bro, you've disappeared. This isn't what love looks like. It's control.' Tushar got defensive, then went silent. Then he admitted he felt like he was walking on eggshells all the time, and that he thought it was his fault for being 'bad at relationships'. 'It's not your fault,' Raghav said. The next morning Tushar sat in the student counselling centre's waiting room, Raghav beside him, filling in the form with shaking hands.

qa.q: How often did Tushar send Kriti a photo?
qa.a: Every hour, to prove where he was.

qa.q: How did Tushar describe feeling in the relationship?
qa.a: He felt anxious and tense, as if walking on eggshells all the time, and wrongly guilty for being 'bad at relationships'.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped?
qa.a: He named the pattern as control, told Tushar it wasn't his fault, and went with him to the counselling centre.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the changes in Tushar?
qa.a: He sees his friend disappearing, quitting the band and skipping birthdays, under control framed as love.

grounding: Shows a young man whose world has shrunk under a partner's control framed as love, recognising it with a friend's help and seeking counselling.

passage: Yamini, you went quiet when Nikhil told us about his fellowship. I know that quiet. Let your Madhuri Mami tell you something. When I was twenty-two, your Mama and I both sat for the bank officer exam. He passed. I didn't. The whole family came with sweets, and I stood in the kitchen feeling like a small dry leaf. I loved him, and I wanted to throw the laddoos at the wall. That night I almost said something cruel: 'Lucky paper, that's all.' It was right there on my tongue. Instead I went up to the terrace and admitted it to myself: I'm jealous. That's allowed. Then I went down and hugged him properly, and meant it. The next month I enrolled for the exam again, and he quizzed me every evening after his training. I passed on my second try. So, child, feel it privately. Celebrate him openly. And then do your own work.

qa.q: What exam did Madhuri and Mama sit for?
qa.a: The bank officer exam.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling in the kitchen while the family celebrated?
qa.a: She felt small and jealous, like a dry leaf, while still loving him.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Madhuri's story?
qa.a: Admitting the jealousy on the terrace, hugging him sincerely, and enrolling for the exam again.

qa.q: How did Mama support Madhuri afterwards?
qa.a: He quizzed her every evening after his training until she passed.

grounding: An elder's story of envying a partner's success, admitting it privately, celebrating him anyway and working on her own path.

passage: The email arrived at 4 p.m.: Farhan's application to the design fellowship had been rejected. At 5, Devika called, breathless. She had topped the university in her law exams and been offered an internship in a senior advocate's chambers. Her family was throwing a dinner that night, in two hours. Farhan said all the right words on the phone, then sat on his bed staring at the wall. He loved her. He also felt about two inches tall. On the drive over, he caught himself rehearsing a joke for the dinner table: 'Well, someone in this couple had to get lucky.' He heard how it would land. He pulled over and sat for a minute. Okay. I'm envious. That's mine to deal with, not hers. At dinner he raised his glass of nimbu pani and gave a real toast about her late nights and stubbornness. Later, alone, he told her about the rejection. She held his hand. On Monday he emailed the fellowship office asking for feedback.

qa.a: The university, in her law exams.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling after Devika's call?
qa.a: He felt envious and small, about two inches tall, even though he loved her.

qa.q: What did Farhan do instead of making the joke?
qa.a: Pulled over, admitted the envy to himself, gave a sincere toast, and later worked on his own path by asking for feedback.

qa.q: How does Devika respond when Farhan tells her about the rejection?
qa.a: She holds his hand, offering support even on her big day.

grounding: Shows a young man envious of his partner's success on the day of his own rejection, admitting it privately, celebrating her and working on his path.
